strengths: The Global Workspace Layer is an interesting synthesis of low-dimensional memory slots, top-k cross-attention, a balancing regularizer, and continuous-Hopfield retrieval. It is modular and adds only about 0.45M parameters per layer.

The principal comparisons show consistent gains over matched ViTs: AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34%, CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, and ImageNet100 from 28.16% to 33.84%. AiT-Medium also slightly exceeds the much larger ViT-Base average while using roughly half its parameters and FLOPs.
Results on Sort-of-CLEVR suggest value for relational reasoning: AiT-Base reaches 80.03% relational accuracy versus 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base.

The paper reports three-run uncertainty for its main small-scale experiments, parameter/FLOP counts, component ablations, initialization and temperature studies, and qualitative analyses of attention diversity and energy.
weaknesses: The batch-global evaluation protocol is a consequential concern. AiT concatenates tokens from every example in a batch and updates memory before reconstructing those examples; Appendix F indicates that this cross-attention remains active at test time. Thus a prediction may depend on unrelated test samples and their batch composition. The manuscript does not establish whether memory is persistent, reset, or only temporarily updated, nor report batch-size-one, reshuffling, or composition controls. This transductive coupling makes comparisons with per-example baselines difficult to interpret.

Several core operations are not mathematically well-defined as written. Because A is defined by softmax, the load term 1[A>0] in Eq. 3 is constant unless an unstated post-top-k mask is intended. The top-k operator and its normalization are unspecified; Eq. 5 contains incompatible or ambiguous matrix products and does not define a scalar or per-token energy clearly; and an argmin is presented as a single update without giving the update rule. Consequently, the claims that all tokens reach a minimum and that energy is guaranteed to decrease after one step are insufficiently supported.

The ablations do not cleanly establish a specific benefit from associative memory. The one-step modern-Hopfield update is closely related to softmax attention, while the “W/O Hopfield” variant substitutes a substantially more expensive learned cross-attention module rather than a parameter- and compute-matched retrieval rule. The observed energy decrease is largely expected from the construction and is not connected empirically to task accuracy.

The sparsity and efficiency claims are overstated. AiT retains dense ViT self-attention and computes the full memory-to-BN score matrix before applying top-k. At matched depth it has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT (e.g., 15.8M/9.64e8 versus 14.9M/9.36e8 for Small), and no latency or peak-memory measurements demonstrate practical sparse-computation benefits.

Experimental evidence has limited external validity. ImageNet100 and Oxford Pet accuracies are very low under the from-scratch recipe, evaluation omits full ImageNet and dense vision tasks, and comparisons largely use older sparse architectures. Sort-of-CLEVR is synthetic, and its Coordination comparison is not parameter matched. Several larger-dataset and relational results lack run-to-run uncertainty.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the stateful mechanism: memory detachment, reset policy, test-time behavior, and synchronization across four GPUs are unspecified. The ImageNet100 subset and several dataset splits are not defined, code is only promised, and the learning rate conflicts between the main text (1e-5) and Table 8 (1e-4). The duplicated CIFAR-10 header in Table 1 is a minor presentation error, but the state-management omissions are material.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: the work primarily combines established memory slots, hard top-k selection, MoE-style balancing, and modern Hopfield/attention retrieval. The experiments do not sufficiently isolate what the Hopfield interpretation contributes beyond this combination. Overall, the empirical merits are worthwhile, but the unresolved protocol and technical-definition issues currently favor rejection.

strengths: The Global Workspace Layer coherently combines low-rank explicit memory, bottleneck attention, and associative retrieval; the architecture is reasonably motivated and modular.
The reported gains are fairly consistent. For example, AiT-Medium reaches an 81.58% average in Table 1 versus 80.46% for ViT-Base, while using 45.9M versus 85.7M parameters.
The ablations provide useful evidence: removing the bottleneck reduces average accuracy from 79.70% to 73.75%, while removing memory, the balance loss, or Hopfield retrieval also hurts performance.
The Sort-of-CLEVR result is promising: AiT-Base obtains 80.03% relational accuracy versus 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base.
The appendix supplies an algorithm, several hyperparameters, attention visualizations, and analyses of memory initialization and inverse temperature.
weaknesses: Material: The model pools all B×N tokens and constructs memory used to reconstruct every sample. As specified, predictions therefore depend on other examples in the test batch; Table 9 indicates that this write attention remains active at test time. There is no evaluation with singleton batches, shuffled batch composition, or independently reset memory, so the gains may partly reflect transductive cross-sample information rather than a fair per-example comparison.

Material: The state semantics are under-specified. The priors are called learnable parameters but are also overwritten through an EWMA across batch time. The paper does not explain optimizer versus EMA updates, gradient detachment, memory initialization/reset boundaries, or whether state persists across evaluation batches. These choices can materially change both correctness and results.

Material: Equations 3–4 do not define a valid trainable load-balancing mechanism as written. The defined softmax scores are strictly positive, making the indicator (A>0) constant; if it instead denotes post-top-k scores, that quantity is not defined and the hard indicator supplies no gradient without an unreported estimator.

Material: The Hopfield formulation is incomplete. Equation 5 writes ΞΞᵀ as part of an energy although this is matrix-valued, and Equation 6 gives an argmin without the actual one-step update or its differentiation rule. Consequently, the claimed simultaneous convergence and guaranteed energy decrease are not established for the implemented layer.

Material: The sparsity and efficiency claims are overstated. Top-k is applied only after computing dense memory-to-token scores, and every block retains dense self-attention. At matched depth, AiT has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT; the favorable efficiency comparison primarily comes from comparing a shallower AiT-Medium with ViT-Base. No latency, peak-memory, or throughput evidence is given.

Material: Evaluation does not adequately substantiate scalability or long-range reasoning. Most experiments use small datasets trained from scratch, relational reasoning is limited to Sort-of-CLEVR, and ImageNet-100, Oxford Pet, and Sort-of-CLEVR lack multi-run uncertainty. The exact ImageNet-100 subset/splits and several test protocols are also unspecified, while comparisons omit stronger contemporary vision-efficient architectures and matched-compute tuning.

Material: The specialization evidence is not causal. Figures 6–8 show one training trajectory without a corresponding no-balance-loss visualization or quantitative comparison, and spatially consistent attention does not by itself demonstrate semantic specialization or improved long-range association.

Reproducibility is presently weak: code is only promised, baseline tuning details and seeds are absent, the main text gives a learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4, and the prose attributes 5.77×10^9 FLOPs to ViT-Base whereas Table 1 assigns 5.60×10^9. Minor prose and figure-density issues are presentation refinements, but these implementation ambiguities are decision-relevant.

strengths: The proposed combination of low-rank workspace priors, hard top-k writing, EWMA memory updates, and modern-Hopfield retrieval is conceptually interesting and potentially useful for contextual representation learning.

Under the reported protocol, AiT consistently improves matched-depth ViTs: AiT-Small reaches 83.34/56.30 versus 79.53/53.19 on CIFAR-10/100, AiT-Medium reaches 36.72 versus 31.72 on ImageNet100, and AiT-Base obtains 80.03 relational accuracy versus 63.35 for ViT-Base and 73.43 for Coordination on Sort-of-CLEVR.

The ablations are reasonably broad. Removing the memory recovers the ViT-Small results, while removing the balance loss, Hopfield retrieval, bottleneck, or self-attention reduces average performance. Memory initialization, test-time attention, inverse-temperature, attention-diversity, and energy analyses provide additional diagnostic evidence.

The main CIFAR/Triangle results average three runs with dispersion, parameters and FLOPs are reported, and the appendix provides many important hyperparameters. The architecture diagram and overall organization are clear.
weaknesses: Material evaluation concern: the workspace flattens all B×N tokens and uses current-batch top-k writes to construct the memory that reconstructs every example. Appendix F confirms that this cross-attention remains active at test time. Consequently, predictions depend on unrelated test examples and possibly evaluation order. For CIFAR, the reported k=512 even exceeds the 65 tokens available at batch size one. No single-image, batch-composition, shuffle, or memory-reset experiment is provided, nor are baselines given equivalent transductive access. Thus the reported numbers do not establish standard per-example classification performance.

Material technical concern: the method is not executable from the equations as written. In Eq. 5, an M×E memory is multiplied by a BN×E token matrix without a transpose, while ΞΞᵀ is matrix-valued rather than a scalar energy. Eq. 6 specifies an exact argmin although the implementation allegedly takes one unspecified update. Algorithm 1 defines A as a strictly positive softmax, making the load term sum_j 1[A>0] constant unless an unreported post-top-k mask is intended. Top-k masking, renormalization, gradients, and EWMA state detachment/persistence are also unspecified.

The evidence supports a depth–accuracy tradeoff, not the broader sparse-computation claim. At every matched depth AiT has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT—for example, 15.8M/0.964G versus 14.9M/0.936G for Small—and Coordination is much smaller. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes the full memory-to-token score matrix before top-k selection. Runtime, peak memory, and scaling with sequence length are not evaluated.

The broad or SOTA claims are insufficiently supported. Evaluation emphasizes small datasets and weak absolute regimes—36.72% on ImageNet100 and 30.05% on Oxford Pet—and compares mainly with older, reimplemented architectures. There is no full ImageNet or CLEVR evaluation and no comparison to contemporary efficient vision Transformers or stronger relational/object-centric methods, including relevant methods cited by the paper.

Reproducibility has consequential gaps: the exact ImageNet100 subset and several dataset splits/batching protocols are absent; most ImageNet100, Pet, and Sort-of-CLEVR results have no uncertainty; the main text gives learning rate 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4; the grid-search space is omitted; and code is only promised for future release.

The Hopfield-specific attribution is not cleanly established. A one-step modern-Hopfield lookup is closely related to attention over stored patterns, while the “W/O Hopfield” replacement changes the model to a substantially more expensive multi-head cross-attention operation, increasing total FLOPs from 0.964G to 1.19G. A matched-cost retrieval baseline is needed to isolate the claimed associative-memory benefit.

Secondary presentation issues include an extensive biological/global-workspace narrative without corresponding empirical or theoretical validation, shifting use of “prior,” “memory,” and “attractor,” and figures whose datasets or uncertainty are sometimes unclear. These refinements are not the main reason for the rating; the batch-dependent evaluation and underspecified formulation are.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent architectural contribution combining low-rank explicit memory, top-k bottleneck attention, and Hopfield-style retrieval for sparse visual representation learning.

The empirical gains are consistent across the principal comparisons. For example, AiT-Small improves over the same-depth ViT-Small on CIFAR-10/100 (83.34/56.30 versus 79.53/53.19) with only 0.9M additional parameters, while AiT-Base substantially improves relational accuracy over ViT-Base and Coordination (80.03 versus 63.35 and 73.43).

The component ablations are useful: removing the bottleneck reduces average accuracy from 79.70 to 73.75, while removing Hopfield retrieval or the balance loss also gives measurable degradation. The initialization, inverse-temperature, energy, and FLOP analyses add diagnostic value.
The manuscript is generally well organized, with an informative architecture diagram, algorithm, hyperparameter appendix, and qualitative visualizations of learned memory slots.
weaknesses: The bottleneck balance loss is technically problematic as written. Because A is defined as a softmax, every A_i,j,o is positive, making the load term sum_j 1(A_i,j,o>0) constant. Even if A is intended to be top-k masked, the hard indicator supplies no gradient. The manuscript does not specify a differentiable estimator, so this component cannot train as claimed.

The Hopfield formulation is dimensionally and operationally underspecified. With the declared shapes, f_LT(gamma)Xi in Eq. 5 cannot be multiplied without transposing Xi, and XiXi^T is a matrix rather than a scalar energy. The actual one-step update is never given, preventing verification of the claimed energy guarantee and faithful reproduction.

The model pools all BN tokens and updates memory from the current batch, so one prediction can depend on unrelated batch members. It is unclear whether memory is updated, reset, or frozen across evaluation batches: the text says it is frozen, while Appendix F shows test-time cross-attention remains active. Batch-composition and order sensitivity are therefore material unresolved concerns, especially since the claimed batch-size robustness is not reported quantitatively.

The evaluation supports proof-of-concept effectiveness but not the manuscript's broad scaling claims. CIFAR, Triangle, Oxford Pet, ImageNet-100, and Sort-of-CLEVR are limited tests; the reported ImageNet-100 and Pet accuracies are low, and the relational comparison omits standard strong baselines such as the original Relation Network and newer reasoning models.

Parameter counts and FLOPs are reported, but not latency, throughput, or memory usage. Several efficiency claims compare a shallower AiT against a deeper ViT rather than compute-matched modern efficient architectures, and the cost implications of batch-wide attention are not adequately assessed.

The specialization evidence is suggestive rather than causal: Figures 6-8 mainly show increasing token coverage and fixed spatial preferences, without a quantitative with-versus-without-balance-loss comparison or evidence that the slots encode semantic or relational specialization rather than positional bias.

Reproducibility is weakened by conflicting learning rates (1e-5 in the main text versus 1e-4 in Table 8), an insufficiently defined ImageNet-100 split, missing uncertainty for several headline results, and code being promised rather than provided. These issues, together with the core formulation ambiguities, keep the otherwise promising work at the decision boundary.

strengths: The central design is coherent and moderately original: the Global Workspace Layer combines low-rank priors, globally top-k memory writing, EWMA updates, and continuous-Hopfield retrieval. Integrating sparse writing with associative reading is a recognizable contribution beyond a routine ViT modification.

The empirical pattern is consistently favorable. AiT-Medium obtains 81.58% average accuracy on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100/Triangle using 45.9M parameters and 2.89×10^9 FLOPs, versus ViT-Base's 80.46% with 85.7M parameters and 5.60×10^9 FLOPs. It also improves ImageNet-100 accuracy from 34.62% to 36.72%, while AiT-Base reaches 80.03% relational accuracy on Sort-of-CLEVR versus 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base.

The ablations provide meaningful internal support. Removing the balance loss, Hopfield retrieval, complete memory layer, or bottleneck lowers the three-task average from 79.70% to 78.68%, 78.48%, 77.40%, and 73.75%, respectively. Memory resetting, initialization, inverse temperature, retrieval energy, and test-time attention are also examined.

The method has potential usefulness as a lightweight enhancement for shallow Transformers, especially in low-data and relational settings. The manuscript is generally organized clearly and includes an architectural diagram, pseudocode, hyperparameters, visual analyses, and an explicit limitations section. Review source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-fu8_sif4/call-b3f0d40e545d42368676c8701f0fbb56/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Material concern: concatenating all B×N tokens, selecting a global top-k set, and broadcasting the resulting memory makes each prediction potentially depend on unrelated samples, batch composition/order, and persistent EWMA state. The manuscript says memory is frozen during evaluation yet reports that test-time writing attention affects accuracy, without specifying whether memory is updated or reset per batch or synchronized across four GPUs. This leaves the inductive-versus-transductive evaluation protocol unresolved.

Material concern: key definitions are technically inconsistent or incomplete as written. Under the stated shapes, f_LT(γ)Ξ and the ΞΞ^T term in the scalar Hopfield energy are dimensionally incompatible, while the claimed one-step minimization lacks an explicit update rule. Moreover, A is defined as a softmax, making 1(A>0) in the load-balancing loss constant; if post-top-k scores were intended, differentiation through the indicator remains unexplained.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. Top-k selection occurs only after dense scores over all B×N tokens have been computed, and ordinary dense self-attention remains; AiT-Base actually requires slightly more FLOPs than ViT-Base, 5.77×10^9 versus 5.60×10^9. The encouraging shallow-model result is not accompanied by matched-parameter controls, runtime, memory-use, or top-k implementation costs.

Evaluation is restricted to comparatively weak from-scratch image baselines and mostly small or synthetic tasks: the best reported CIFAR-10, ImageNet-100, and Oxford Pet accuracies are approximately 85%, 37%, and 30%. There is no ImageNet-1K experiment, strong DeiT-style training recipe, modern efficient Transformer comparison, or canonical Relation Network comparison on Sort-of-CLEVR, limiting the breadth of the conclusions.

Attribution among components is incomplete. The no-Hopfield control substitutes a substantially heavier multi-head cross-attention rather than a parameter/FLOP-matched single-step memory-attention operation. Likewise, specialization is visualized over training epochs but not compared directly against a model without the balance loss, so the figures do not isolate the claimed causal mechanism.

Reproducibility details require correction: the main text specifies a 10^-5 learning rate while Table 8 gives 10^-4; the exact ImageNet-100 subset and memory synchronization/detachment procedures are absent; several result tables lack uncertainty; and code is only promised. These are largely correctable presentation and reporting issues rather than independent grounds for rejection.

strengths: The proposed combination of low-rank memory slots, top-k bottleneck attention, and Hopfield-style retrieval is relevant to efficient visual representation learning and potentially useful. The overall architecture is presented clearly in the manuscript. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2x3x7ffa/call-9a56e167640646dcbfd71aab7a45319d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Matched-backbone results show consistent gains over vanilla ViT: AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, while AiT-Medium improves ImageNet100 from 31.72% to 36.72%.
The Sort-of-CLEVR relational result is promising: AiT-Base reaches 80.03%, compared with 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base under the reported setup.

The paper includes several useful analyses, including component ablations, parameter/FLOP counts, initialization comparisons, test-time attention ablation, temperature sensitivity, and visualizations of memory-slot behavior. Primary CIFAR/Triangle tables report means and variability over three runs.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: the associative-memory computation is not mathematically well specified. Given the declared shapes, f_LT(gamma)Xi in Eq. 5 is dimensionally invalid without a transpose, while XiXi^T is a matrix rather than a per-token scalar energy. Eq. 6 merely states an argmin, yet the implementation reportedly takes one update step without providing that update, step size, or closed form. Consequently, the central Hopfield operation and its convergence claim cannot be verified or reproduced from the paper.

Material technical issue: the proposed balance loss appears ineffective as written. A_i is defined as a softmax and is therefore positive at every position, making the load term sum_j 1(A_i,j,o>0) constant and its variance zero. If A_i instead denotes post-top-k masked scores, that conflicts with the earlier definition, and the hard indicator remains nondifferentiable without a stated surrogate. This directly affects a claimed methodological contribution.

The model is intrinsically coupled to arbitrary batch composition: all BxN tokens are concatenated, memory is updated at each batch time step, and the fixed top-k is selected across samples. It is unclear how memory updates interact with the statement that memory is frozen at evaluation, or how state is synchronized across four GPUs. For CIFAR, k=512 exceeds the number of tokens in single-image inference, so the bottleneck becomes dense or undefined. The unsupported statement that batch size has little effect does not resolve prediction dependence on co-batched examples or ordering.

The broad efficiency claim is not established. Every block retains full self-attention, and dense memory-token scores must be computed before top-k selection. At matched depth, AiT is larger and uses more FLOPs than ViT; for example, AiT-Base uses 91.0M parameters and 5.77G FLOPs versus 85.7M and 5.60G for ViT-Base. The paper provides no latency, peak-memory, or scaling measurements, so the evidence supports accuracy gains at selected operating points rather than general computational efficiency.

The evaluation does not substantiate the claimed broad or state-of-the-art impact. It is dominated by small datasets and very low-accuracy from-scratch regimes, while ImageNet100 lacks a defined class subset and full ImageNet or downstream vision tasks are absent. Several baselines are old or not competitive image classifiers, and the standard Relation Network from the cited Sort-of-CLEVR source paper is omitted. ImageNet100, Oxford Pet, and Sort-of-CLEVR results also lack uncertainty estimates.

The ablations establish that the complete implementation performs better, but do not validate the proposed explanations. Replacing Hopfield retrieval with a substantially more expensive cross-attention module is not a controlled alternative; guaranteed energy reduction does not demonstrate useful associative recall; and no noisy/partial-pattern retrieval or capacity experiment is given. Likewise, the slot visualizations mainly show fixed spatial-position preferences, which could arise from positional embeddings, and no loss-disabled visualization demonstrates that the balance loss causes specialization.

Originality is only moderately supported. Learned latent queries and cross-attention are closely related to Set Transformer, Perceiver, Slot Attention, and TokenLearner; a one-step modern Hopfield update is closely related to ordinary attention; and the importance/load coefficient-of-variation objective resembles established mixture-of-experts balancing losses. The paper presents a potentially useful integration, but does not clearly isolate a fundamentally new mechanism from these antecedents.

Reproducibility has consequential gaps: the main text gives an initial learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4; no grid-search ranges or validation protocol are specified; the ImageNet100 subset and Sort-of-CLEVR split are not defined; and top-k masking/renormalization, gradient handling through memory updates, distributed memory synchronization, and evaluation-state behavior are omitted. Code is only promised for future release. These issues, together with the mathematical ambiguities and batch-coupled protocol, outweigh the otherwise promising empirical gains. Minor wording and equation-reference errors are presentation refinements and do not determine the rating.

strengths: The central idea is coherent and potentially useful: low-dimensional persistent slots perform top-k writes, followed by a modern-Hopfield readout inside ViT blocks. The shared-memory motivation and architecture are understandable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-398a2qqq/call-4a8a331f865e4d1395fd3c2aa8a48865/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The controlled comparisons show consistent gains over matched ViTs: AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10/100 from 79.53/53.19 to 83.34/56.30, while AiT-Medium improves them from 82.41/55.78 to 84.59/60.58. It also improves ImageNet100 accuracy from 31.72 to 36.72 at comparable size.

The component study is reasonably broad. Removing the bottleneck, memory, Hopfield readout, balance loss, or self-attention reduces the reported average, and the complete model performs best. Parameter counts and FLOPs are also reported.
The high-level presentation is organized, with a useful overview figure, pseudocode, hyperparameter table, initialization study, inverse-temperature sweep, and qualitative attention visualizations.
weaknesses: The test protocol for the persistent memory is materially ambiguous. The paper says memory is frozen during evaluation, but Appendix F reports a test-time effect from disabling the write cross-attention, implying that test examples still update memory. Because all BxN tokens are pooled, predictions may then depend on other test samples, their order, batch size, and prior test batches. Moreover, k=512 exceeds the token count of a single CIFAR or Pet image, so ordinary single-image inference is undefined without an unreported modification. This prevents treating the reported accuracies as clearly standard independent-sample evaluation.

Important mathematical details are inconsistent or invalid as written. In Eq. (5), an MxE attractor matrix is multiplied by a BNxE token matrix without a transpose, and Xi Xi^T is matrix-valued although the energy should be scalar or per-token. Eq. (6) specifies an argmin, whereas the implementation reportedly takes one update step, which generally does not reach that argmin. The actual closed-form Hopfield update, masking, top-k renormalization, residual path, and state-detachment behavior are not specified.

The proposed load-balancing term is problematic. A is defined as a softmax and is therefore strictly positive, making sum_j 1[A_{i,j,o}>0] constant. If A instead denotes post-top-k weights, this needs to be stated, and the hard indicator remains nondifferentiable with zero gradient absent a surrogate or straight-through rule. Thus one of the two claimed loss components cannot train the model under the presented formulation.

The efficiency claims are overstated. AiT retains dense self-attention and computes dense memory-to-token scores before applying top-k, so it does not remove the backbone's quadratic attention cost. At matched depth it is slightly larger and more expensive than ViT—for example, 15.8M/0.964G versus 14.9M/0.936G for Small. The results support an accuracy/parameter tradeoff relative to a deeper ViT, but not computational sparsity or scalable efficiency; no latency, memory, or high-resolution scaling measurements are provided.

The evidence is insufficient for the broad SOTA and long-range-reasoning claims. Most experiments use small datasets, ImageNet100 accuracy is very low, and Oxford Pet peaks near 30%. Comparisons omit stronger contemporary vision transformers and token-pruning/sparse-attention methods. There is no ImageNet-1K or dense-prediction evaluation, and ImageNet100 and Sort-of-CLEVR results lack uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility has consequential gaps: the main text gives an initial learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4; the ImageNet100 class subset and split are unspecified; memory initialization/reset at evaluation, cross-device synchronization for the pooled batch on four GPUs, random seeds, and exact baseline tuning are not documented; and code is only promised for future release.

The specialization evidence is largely qualitative and lacks controls. Increasing diversity over training is not compared with a model without the balance loss, and attending to consistent absolute patch positions can be explained by positional embeddings rather than semantic specialization. No controlled test measures long-range generalization. Overall, promising gains and useful ablations remain, but the stateful evaluation ambiguity and formulation problems currently make the scientific support inadequate for acceptance.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for CVPR 2025.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess technical correctness, the evidence supporting the claims, contribution to computer vision or pattern recognition, originality, potential usefulness, clarity, and reproducibility. Weigh scientific strengths and limitations together. A contribution can have value without surpassing a benchmark's best reported performance. Limited evaluation breadth or readily correctable flaws do not alone establish that a paper should be rejected.

Give specific, evidence-supported reasons for the recommendation. Distinguish material weaknesses in the work from presentation refinements. Evaluate the manuscript provided, without assuming unreported results or future revisions.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5.

Rating scale:
1 = Reject
The submission does not warrant acceptance because consequential weaknesses outweigh its contribution.

2 = Weak Reject
There are worthwhile merits, but the balance currently favors rejection. Identify the concerns that determine this direction.

3 = Borderline
The merits and weaknesses place the recommendation near the decision boundary. Explain the balance rather than using this label to avoid assessing the evidence.

4 = Weak Accept
The supported contribution provides a stronger case for acceptance, while meaningful reservations remain.

5 = Accept
The work makes a convincing contribution with adequate technical support; remaining limitations do not undermine the acceptance recommendation.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

The headline savings arise by comparing a six-block AiT against a twelve-block ViT. There is no throughput, activation-memory, or sequence-length scaling study.

Experimental support is weak for the breadth of the claims. ImageNet-100 compares only against ViT and reaches 36.72%; Oxford Pet reaches about 30% and is shown mainly as a training curve. Neither has uncertainty estimates. The classification baselines are largely older methods, and there is no full ImageNet or modern efficient-vision comparison. Sort-of-CLEVR omits the canonical Relation Network from the cited dataset paper and does not evaluate on the harder CLEVR benchmark, so the claimed state of the art and complex relational reasoning are not established.

The mechanistic evidence is insufficient. Diversity is plotted only across epochs, not against a model trained without the balance loss. The reported specialization largely consists of slots selecting fixed spatial positions across images, which may follow directly from positional embeddings and does not demonstrate semantic specialization or long-range association. Energy reduction is expected from the chosen Hopfield update, and no noisy/partial-pattern recall experiment establishes associative retrieval.

Reproducibility details conflict or are absent: the main text specifies an initial learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4; the meaning of the reported plus/minus values is undefined; ImageNet-100 construction and splits are not described; grid-search ranges and baseline-specific tuning are omitted; and code is only promised. Minor language and cross-reference issues are secondary to these technical and empirical concerns.

The individual ingredients - learned latent queries, top-k gating, load balancing, EWMA memory, and modern Hopfield/attention retrieval - are established techniques. Their integration is potentially useful, but the paper does not yet demonstrate a sufficiently distinct principle or rigorous empirical advantage to overcome the issues above. The worthwhile idea and positive ablations justify weak rather than unequivocal rejection, but the current balance favors rejection.

strengths: AiT is an interesting synthesis of low-dimensional priors, top-k memory writing, EWMA updates, and a modern-Hopfield read operation. The module is lightweight and the high-level architecture is clearly illustrated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ss8hbe59/call-f42033566c144f3f824e1dd90adba831/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Controlled same-depth comparisons show a consistent empirical signal. For example, AiT-Small improves over ViT-Small from 79.53% to 83.34% on CIFAR-10 and from 53.19% to 56.30% on CIFAR-100 with only 0.9M additional parameters; AiT-Medium similarly improves ImageNet100 accuracy from 31.72% to 36.72%.

The component study is relatively thorough: it examines removal of memory, bottlenecking, the balance loss, Hopfield retrieval, and self-attention, as well as memory resetting, initialization, inverse temperature, and test-time attention. Removing the complete workspace reduces CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 accuracy to 79.53%/53.19%, while the full model obtains 83.34%/56.30%.

Results on relational Sort-of-CLEVR are promising against the selected Transformer baselines: AiT-Base obtains 80.03% relational accuracy versus 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base. The paper also reports parameters, FLOPs, and three-run variability for its principal small-dataset experiments.
weaknesses: The evaluation is fundamentally batch-dependent. The workspace pools all B×N tokens across different images, and the chosen k exceeds the number of tokens in one image—for example, k=512 versus 65 CIFAR tokens and approximately 196 Oxford-Pet/ImageNet tokens. Thus the reported configuration cannot perform ordinary single-image inference and each prediction can depend on unrelated co-batched test examples. Appendix F confirms that test-time cross-attention affects accuracy, yet there is no evaluation of batch size one, batch composition, ordering, shuffling, or state persistence. This prevents interpreting the reported numbers as standard inductive classification results and could favor AiT over per-image baselines through test-batch structure.

The proposed balance loss is technically problematic as written. A_i is defined as a softmax and is therefore positive at every position, making the load term sum_j 1(A_i,j,o>0)=M with zero variance. If A_i instead denotes the hard top-k-masked scores, the indicator has zero gradient almost everywhere; no straight-through or differentiable load estimator is specified. Consequently, one of the two claimed balancing components cannot train the model under the stated equations.

The associative retrieval is insufficiently specified. Equation 5 contains dimensionally incompatible products unless omitted transposes and reductions are supplied, Algorithm 1 expresses an exact argmin while the implementation reportedly performs one iteration, and the actual update rule is absent. The claim that all tokens reach a minimum after one step is not justified. Moreover, a one-step modern-Hopfield update is mathematically a form of prototype cross-attention, but the provided cross-attention ablation is not parameter- or FLOP-matched, weakening both novelty and causal attribution.

The computational-efficiency claim is overstated. AiT retains dense ViT self-attention and adds the workspace; at matched depth it uses more parameters and FLOPs than ViT (e.g., 15.8M/0.964B versus 14.9M/0.936B for the small models). Top-k is applied only after dense memory-to-token scores are formed. No latency, peak-memory, or multi-GPU communication measurements are given, although cross-sample pooling may require substantial synchronization.

The empirical scope does not adequately support the broad superiority and practical-efficiency claims. Triangle is saturated, Sort-of-CLEVR is synthetic, and the ImageNet100 and Oxford-Pet accuracies are low under a weak from-scratch recipe. There is no full ImageNet or downstream detection/segmentation evaluation, no recent vision-specific sparse or token-pruning baselines, and Table 6 omits the Relation Network from the cited Sort-of-CLEVR work. The fixed-width, variable-depth ViT comparisons also do not establish a well-tuned parameter-efficiency frontier.

Important reproducibility details conflict or are missing: the main text gives an initial learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4; the ImageNet100 class subset and preprocessing are unspecified; top-k masking and renormalization are unclear; and the interaction between learnable priors, stateful EWMA updates, gradient detachment, distributed synchronization, and the claim that memory is frozen at evaluation is not explained. Code is only promised for future release.

The qualitative analysis does not establish the claimed mechanism. Diversity and specialization figures show evolution over epochs but not comparisons without the balance loss, so the effect cannot be attributed to that loss; spatially consistent maps could arise from positional embeddings. Likewise, guaranteed Hopfield-energy reduction does not demonstrate semantic retrieval or long-range reasoning. These issues, especially the nonstandard batch-conditioned evaluation and ambiguities in the core method, outweigh the worthwhile architectural idea and favor weak rejection.

strengths: The manuscript proposes a coherent combination of low-rank explicit memory, top-k workspace attention, and continuous-Hopfield retrieval that can be inserted into a ViT block. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-afe7410p/call-019be6f98b22482486df0115cf6bef87/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The same-depth CIFAR comparisons show consistent gains over ViT: AiT-S improves CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 from 79.53/53.19 to 83.34/56.30, with analogous gains for the Medium and Base variants.
The Sort-of-CLEVR relational result is encouraging: AiT-Base reaches 80.03%, compared with 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base under the reported setup.

The component ablations are useful: removing memory lowers the three-task average from 79.70 to 77.40, while removing Hopfield retrieval, the balance loss, or the bottleneck also degrades it. Most reported CIFAR results include variation over three runs.
The reported AiT-Medium point is practically interesting: it slightly exceeds ViT-Base's three-task average while using approximately half its parameters and FLOPs.
weaknesses: Material technical concern: the proposed load-balancing term is ineffective as written. Since A is defined as a dense softmax, every A_i,j,o is positive and the indicator sum in the load term is constant. If A instead denotes the hard top-k-masked scores, the indicator is non-differentiable almost everywhere. No relaxation or straight-through estimator is specified, and masking and renormalization are also ambiguous.

Material evaluation concern: the architecture pools all samples in a batch and updates memory by EWMA. Appendix F indicates that this cross-attention remains important at test time, despite the main text calling evaluation memory frozen. Consequently, predictions may depend on test-batch composition, order, and preceding test samples. The reported k also exceeds the number of tokens in a single image on several datasets, precluding the stated configuration from ordinary single-image inference. Reset policy and batch-size sensitivity are not evaluated.

The Hopfield formulation is insufficiently specified and dimensionally inconsistent for batched tokens: Equation 5 omits a needed transpose, combines matrix-valued terms without stating reductions, and Equation 6 gives an argmin rather than the actual one-step update used. The claim that all tokens reach their minima after the stated single step is not justified by the manuscript.

The evidence does not support the broad or SOTA framing. Comparisons are mainly against older or weakly performing reimplementations; no contemporary efficient vision Transformer baselines are included. The largest classification experiment is only ImageNet100, with 36.72% accuracy, and Sort-of-CLEVR omits stronger relational architectures. These omissions matter because general efficiency and relational-reasoning superiority are central claims.

The efficiency interpretation is incomplete. At matched depth, every AiT variant has more parameters and FLOPs than its ViT counterpart; AiT also retains dense self-attention and computes dense memory-token scores before top-k selection. The attractive comparison instead uses a six-layer AiT against a twelve-layer ViT. No latency, memory-use, or throughput measurements establish a practical sparse-computation advantage.

The Hopfield ablation replaces retrieval with substantially more expensive multi-head cross-attention, increasing total FLOPs from 9.64e8 to 1.19e9, so it does not isolate an associative-memory benefit. Likewise, the specialization visualizations lack a no-balance-loss comparison, repetitions, or quantitative slot-diversity statistics, and the energy analysis presents only a limited example.

Reproducibility has consequential gaps: the main text specifies a 1e-5 initial learning rate while Table 8 specifies 1e-4; the persistence and gradient treatment of the supposedly learnable EWMA memory are unclear; the ImageNet100 class subset is undefined; validation and grid-search protocols are absent; several datasets lack uncertainty estimates; and code is only promised rather than supplied. These issues affect interpretation of the results, not merely presentation polish.

strengths: The proposed combination of low-dimensional explicit memory, top-k memory writing, a balancing regularizer, and Hopfield-style retrieval is a coherent architectural idea that could be useful as a lightweight Transformer augmentation.

The matched comparisons show consistent gains over ViTs of the same depth: for example, AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 accuracy from 79.53/53.19 to 83.34/56.30 with modest additional parameters. AiT-Medium also slightly exceeds ViT-Base's reported average while using roughly half the parameters and FLOPs.
The Sort-of-CLEVR relational result is promising: AiT-Base reaches 80.03%, compared with 73.43% for Coordination under the reported setup.

The component ablations are useful and directionally consistent. Removing the balance loss, Hopfield retrieval, or bottleneck reduces average accuracy from 79.70% to 78.68%, 78.48%, and 73.75%, respectively. The manuscript also examines initialization, inverse temperature, test-time attention, and memory specialization.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes an informative architecture diagram, algorithm description, hyperparameter table, and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: Material—evaluation protocol: AiT concatenates tokens from every sample in a batch and uses them to update a shared memory before broadcasting it back to individual samples. It is unclear whether this update persists, is reset, or is merely detached during evaluation. Appendix F indicates that cross-attention remains active at test time, despite the main text saying memory is frozen. Consequently, predictions may depend on test-batch composition and order, making comparisons with independently evaluated baselines potentially non-equivalent. The unsupported statement that batch size has little effect does not resolve this concern.

Material—technical specification: as written, the selected-instance loss is defective. A is defined as the output of softmax, so every A[i,j,o] is positive and the indicator A[i,j,o] > 0 is always one; its variance and contribution to the loss are therefore zero. If A instead denotes top-k-masked scores, the masking, normalization, and notation needed to reproduce the loss are missing.

Material—Hopfield formulation: Equation 6 defines an exact argmin, whereas the implementation allegedly performs one update, but the actual update rule is never given. Equation 5 also applies products and quadratic terms to the full token matrix in ways inconsistent with the declared shapes. Thus neither the claimed energy descent nor the implemented retrieval can be verified from the manuscript.

Material—efficiency claims are overstated: every AiT block retains dense self-attention, and the method computes dense memory-to-token scores before applying top-k. At matched depth, AiT has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT; its favorable efficiency comparison primarily comes from choosing a shallower AiT. No latency, peak-memory, throughput, or sequence-length scaling measurements establish practical sparse-attention efficiency.

The evaluation is not sufficiently representative for the breadth of the claims. It is dominated by CIFAR, Triangle, Oxford Pet, and Sort-of-CLEVR; ImageNet100 is the largest experiment but its subset construction is unspecified and its absolute accuracy is only 36.72%. Full-scale recognition and stronger contemporary efficient-vision baselines are absent. Pet, ImageNet100, and Sort-of-CLEVR results also lack uncertainty estimates.

Originality is moderate. Low-dimensional inducing memories and write/read cross-attention are established in Perceiver, Set Transformer, and Luna, while a one-step modern Hopfield retrieval is closely related to softmax attention over stored patterns. The paper does not provide a compute- and parameter-matched test showing that the Hopfield formulation itself is preferable to an equivalent tied attention layer.

Reproducibility has consequential gaps: the learning rate is 1e-5 in the main text but 1e-4 in Table 8; the prose assigns 5.77×10^9 FLOPs to ViT-Base while Table 1 reports 5.60×10^9; ImageNet100 classes and splits, grid-search ranges, memory-state/autograd handling, and exact top-k behavior are not specified; and code is only promised.

The specialization evidence is largely anecdotal. The diversity visualizations show changes over training but do not compare against training without the balance loss, and attending to fixed spatial positions does not by itself demonstrate semantic specialization or long-range relational association. Overall, the empirical improvements are worthwhile, but the ambiguous batch-dependent inference and technically incomplete objective/retrieval definitions make the current evidence insufficient for acceptance.

strengths: The proposed Global Workspace Layer is a coherent combination of low-rank priors, top-k bottleneck attention, exponential memory updates, and associative retrieval. The batch-level workspace is an interesting architectural idea with potential utility beyond the evaluated tasks.

The reported gains over the authors' ViT baselines are meaningful: AiT-Medium exceeds ViT-Base on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 while using roughly half the parameters and FLOPs, and AiT-Base improves relational Sort-of-CLEVR accuracy from 63.35% to 80.03%.

The paper includes useful ablations of the bottleneck, balance loss, Hopfield component, self-attention, memory reset, initialization, and inverse temperature. Results are averaged over three runs for the main small-scale classification experiments, and parameter/FLOP counts are reported.
The visualizations of selected patches, memory-slot specialization, and energy evolution provide intuition about the intended behavior, even though they do not fully validate the causal claims.
weaknesses: The most consequential concern is the evaluation protocol. Tokens from the entire batch are concatenated and used to update persistent memory. Although Section 3.2 says memory is frozen during evaluation, Appendix F shows that disabling cross-attention specifically at test time changes accuracy, including 30.05% to 28.68% on Oxford Pet and 76.82% to 75.17% on relational reasoning. This implies that test examples update memory and affect one another. Predictions therefore depend on test-batch composition, order, batch size, and preceding test data, unlike the baselines. No fixed-memory, batch-size-one, reset-per-batch, or order-sensitivity results are provided, so the reported improvements cannot be interpreted as standard independent-sample evaluation.

Several central equations are not technically well-defined as written. In Eq. 5, f_LT(gamma) has shape M-by-E and Xi has shape BN-by-E, making their displayed product invalid; Xi Xi^T is a BN-by-BN matrix rather than a scalar energy. Equation 6 denotes an exact argmin while the implementation allegedly takes one update, but that update is never specified. In the balance loss, A is defined as a softmax and is therefore strictly positive, making the load count in Eq. 3 constant; if post-top-k scores were intended, the indicator remains nondifferentiable absent an unreported surrogate. These are central algorithmic issues, not cosmetic notation errors.

The memory's optimization and state semantics are insufficiently specified. Gamma is simultaneously called learnable and updated by EWMA across batches, without explaining gradient flow, detachment, initialization before evaluation, reset rules, or synchronization across four GPUs. Top-k masking and renormalization are also unspecified. The main text gives a learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4, and code is only promised rather than supplied.

The evidence supports efficiency only relative to a deeper ViT under this particular weak training recipe. AiT adds parameters and FLOPs at matched depth and is much larger than Coordination in Table 1. Oxford Pet and ImageNet100 accuracies are only about 30% and 37%, respectively; the evaluation omits full ImageNet, dense vision tasks, modern efficient vision architectures, throughput, and memory measurements. Consequently, the broad parameter-efficiency and vision-utility claims are overstated.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed associative-memory contribution. Modern continuous Hopfield retrieval is closely related to softmax attention, while the 'W/O Hopfield' replacement has substantially greater FLOPs and is not computation- or parameter-matched. Likewise, the specialization figures only show evolution over training rather than a controlled comparison with and without the balance loss. Overall, the architectural idea and empirical signals are worthwhile, but the stateful test protocol and underspecified mathematics currently prevent confidence in the conclusions.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent architectural idea combining low-rank explicit memory, top-k bottleneck attention, a balancing objective, and Hopfield-style retrieval. Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 communicate the intended data flow reasonably well. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rno086mf/call-da32df36ec0549249423a363a4f7d465/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The primary CIFAR/Triangle results report three-run means and deviations, and AiT consistently improves over matched-depth ViT variants. The component ablations also generally support contributions from the memory, bottleneck, balancing loss, and retrieval components.

There is some credible parameter-performance evidence: AiT-Medium reports 81.58% average accuracy with 45.9M parameters and 2.89e9 FLOPs, versus 80.46% with 85.7M parameters and 5.60e9 FLOPs for ViT-Base.
The Sort-of-CLEVR relational result is promising: AiT-Base reaches 80.03%, compared with 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base.
weaknesses: A material inconsistency makes the evaluation protocol difficult to trust. Section 3.2 says the explicit memory is frozen during evaluation, but Appendix F reports that disabling the cross-attention memory-writing operation at test time lowers accuracy. Under the stated architecture, that operation only affects the memory update. If test batches do update memory, predictions depend on test-batch composition and order; if memory is truly frozen, the reported test-time ablation should have no effect. This must be resolved to establish that the reported evaluation is standard and leakage-free.

The architecture intrinsically mixes tokens across all samples in a batch. The fixed bottleneck is selected from BN tokens, with k=512 for CIFAR and Pets, yet no single-image inference rule is given when BN<k. There is also no meaningful batch-size/composition sensitivity experiment despite the claim that batch size has little effect. This significantly limits deployability and reproducibility.

The proposed balancing loss is not technically well specified. Equation 3 defines the load term using 1(A_i,j,o>0). Before top-k masking, softmax scores are strictly positive, making this term constant; after masking, the indicator is non-differentiable. The manuscript neither defines which scores are used nor provides a gradient estimator. It also omits whether retained top-k weights are renormalized. Thus, a central claimed contribution cannot be implemented unambiguously.

The Hopfield formulation contains consequential mathematical ambiguities: the products in Equation 5 are dimensionally inconsistent as written, Xi Xi^T is a matrix rather than a scalar energy, and Equation 6 states an exact argmin while the implementation allegedly performs one update step without specifying that update. Moreover, a one-step modern Hopfield update is closely related to softmax attention, and the higher-cost multi-head cross-attention replacement does not isolate whether the claimed benefit comes specifically from associative-memory dynamics.

The efficiency claims are overstated. Every AiT block retains dense self-attention, so the method does not remove the quadratic token-token operation. Only theoretical FLOPs and parameter counts are reported, with no throughput, latency, peak-memory, or sequence-length scaling measurements. Several supposedly parameter-efficient baselines are much smaller than AiT-Small, while the favorable comparison instead contrasts a six-layer AiT with a twelve-layer ViT.

The evidence is not sufficiently representative for the breadth of the claims. Most experiments use CIFAR, a synthetic Triangle task, or Sort-of-CLEVR; ImageNet100 compares only against ViT and reaches a low 36.72% accuracy, while Oxford Pets is around 30%. There is no full-scale visual benchmark, long-sequence setting, or contemporary competitive training recipe demonstrating that the gains survive outside weak from-scratch baselines.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. Architectures range from 2.2M to 91.0M parameters, several reimplementations perform unusually poorly, and the paper only states that author-recommended settings were used rather than showing comparable tuning or compute budgets. ImageNet100, Pets, and relational results lack the three-run uncertainty reported in Table 1.

Reproduction is currently doubtful: code is only promised for future release; the main text gives a learning rate of 1e-5 whereas Table 8 gives 1e-4; and important details such as memory-state mutation, evaluation initialization, data ordering, ImageNet100 subset construction, top-k differentiation, and the explicit Hopfield update are absent. These are material omissions rather than presentation refinements.

The integration is potentially useful, but its individual ingredients are established techniques and the paper does not convincingly distinguish the one-step Hopfield retrieval from attention or position the balancing objective against prior load-balancing losses. Together with the unresolved evaluation semantics and limited evidence, the worthwhile empirical signal is not yet sufficient for acceptance.

strengths: The Global Workspace Layer is a coherent architectural proposal combining low-rank explicit memory, top-k bottleneck attention, a balancing objective, and Hopfield-style retrieval. This integration is potentially useful for studying sparse, memory-mediated representations.

Matched-depth comparisons show consistent gains over ViT: AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%, while adding only 0.9M parameters. AiT-Medium also exceeds ViT-Base's reported average accuracy with roughly half the FLOPs.

The component ablations are informative. Removing memory recovers the ViT baseline, while removing the bottleneck, balance loss, or Hopfield retrieval degrades performance; the reported Hopfield read is also substantially cheaper than the cross-attention replacement.

The complete manuscript is organized and visually clear, with an architectural overview, pseudocode, hyperparameter table, attention visualizations, and energy analysis. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-t2b3bov6/call-6383bb90c7e84d09aab72af551f07f16/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: A material concern is that the method couples examples across the batch: attention selects from all B×N tokens, and Appendix F indicates this attention remains active at test time. Consequently, a prediction depends on unrelated co-batched test images. Moreover, the stated CIFAR bottleneck k=512 exceeds the approximately 65 tokens available for batch-size-one inference. No single-image protocol, batch-composition/order robustness study, or clearly disclosed transductive evaluation protocol is provided, so comparison with independently evaluated ViTs is difficult to interpret.

Parts of the central formulation are not technically well-defined. Equation 5 multiplies an M×E attractor matrix by a BN×E token matrix without a transpose and uses ΞΞᵀ, a matrix, as though it were scalar energy. More substantively, Equation 3 thresholds the softmax scores A>0; mathematically every softmax entry is positive, making the load term constant. If A instead denotes post-top-k scores, the binary indicator is non-differentiable. The manuscript also claims tokens reach their minima although only one Hopfield update is used. Missing transposes or reductions are editorially repairable, but the loss-gradient and convergence claims require technical clarification.

The efficiency claims are overstated. Every AiT block retains dense self-attention, and top-k is applied only after computing dense memory-to-token scores. At equal depth, AiT has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT; the claimed savings arise from comparing a shallower AiT with a deeper, poorly performing ViT. There are no latency, peak-memory, throughput, or long-sequence scaling measurements demonstrating computational sparsity.

The evaluation offers limited evidence for broad computer-vision usefulness. Most results use CIFAR, Triangle, or Sort-of-CLEVR; Oxford Pet and ImageNet100 accuracies are very low, and ImageNet100 has only ViT comparisons without uncertainty. The relational comparison omits the original Relation Network and newer reasoning methods, while the vision study omits modern token-selection, token-merging, efficient-attention, and compact-ViT baselines. Thus, outperforming the selected older sparse models does not establish the stated SOTA positioning.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate. Section 4.1 specifies an initial learning rate of 1e-5 whereas Table 8 gives 1e-4; the ImageNet100 class subset and preprocessing are not defined; the grid-search space and validation protocol are absent; and it is unclear whether EWMA memory is an optimizer parameter or detached state, how it is frozen at evaluation, and how batch-global memory updates are synchronized across four GPUs. The code is only promised for future release.

Most uncertainty estimates are confined to Table 1 and use only three runs without defining whether ± denotes standard deviation or standard error. Sort-of-CLEVR, ImageNet100, Oxford Pet, and several diagnostic plots lack uncertainty. Key sensitivities—batch size and composition, bottleneck capacity, memory rank/slot count, update ordering, and Hopfield iteration count—are not evaluated despite being central to the mechanism.

The originality is moderate rather than decisive: modern Hopfield retrieval is closely related to attention with tied keys and values, while latent memory, bottleneck attention, and load-balancing objectives are established ideas. The particular combination is novel and promising, but the technical ambiguities and evaluation protocol currently prevent the contribution from supporting acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6bchtcl5/call-3b0befedbbe942a69c8f81ea4756bfae/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents an interesting modular combination of low-rank explicit memory, top-k bottleneck attention, and continuous-Hopfield retrieval. The Global Workspace Layer is lightweight at roughly 0.45M parameters per layer and could be useful beyond the evaluated tasks.

Results show consistent improvements over matched-depth ViTs: AiT-Small improves CIFAR-10 from 79.53% to 83.34% and CIFAR-100 from 53.19% to 56.30%; AiT-Medium improves them from 82.41% to 84.59% and 55.78% to 60.58%. Improvements also appear on ImageNet100 and Sort-of-CLEVR relational questions.

The main CIFAR/Triangle table reports three-run variation, and the component ablations cover persistent memory, the balance loss, Hopfield retrieval, the bottleneck, and self-attention. Removing the complete workspace recovers the corresponding ViT result, making the principal comparison interpretable.
The paper is generally well organized and visually clear, with an algorithm, hyperparameter table, computational statistics, and qualitative analyses of attention specialization and Hopfield energy.
weaknesses: A central evaluation ambiguity is consequential: tokens from all examples in a batch are concatenated, and the explicit memory is updated across batch time by EWMA, yet the paper also says memory is frozen during evaluation while reporting a test-time write-attention ablation. It never establishes whether test predictions depend on preceding test samples or current batch composition, nor reports reset, ordering, batch-size-one, or multi-GPU synchronization controls. This potentially makes the benchmark evaluation transductive and not directly comparable to per-image baselines.

The balance loss is not technically valid as written. The defined softmax scores A are strictly positive, so the selected-instance term sum_j 1[A_i,j,o>0] is constant for every token; even if A denotes a post-top-k mask, the indicator is nondifferentiable and supplies no gradient absent an unstated estimator. The precise masked attention and gradient treatment are not specified.

The Hopfield formulation is dimensionally and algorithmically incomplete. In Eq. 5, an M-by-E attractor matrix is multiplied by an (BN)-by-E token matrix without a transpose, while the quadratic term is matrix-valued rather than a scalar energy. Eq. 6 states an argmin although the implementation allegedly takes one update, but that update is never given. Together with unclear detachment and persistence of the EWMA state, the manuscript does not define a reproducible forward/training procedure.

Evidence specifically attributing gains to associative memory is weak. One-step modern Hopfield retrieval is closely related to attention, while the 'W/O Hopfield' control replaces it with a larger multi-head cross-attention module and raises total FLOPs from 0.964B to 1.19B, so it is not parameter- or compute-matched. Resetting memory changes the three-task average by only 0.58 points, and disabling write attention at test changes CIFAR-10/100 and Triangle by at most 0.09 points, weakening the claimed mechanism on the main classification tasks.

The efficiency claim is overstated. AiT retains dense self-attention in every block and adds the workspace; at matched depth it has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT (e.g., 45.9M/2.89B versus 42.7M/2.81B for Medium). Comparisons against deeper ViTs demonstrate a useful accuracy-depth tradeoff, but not replacement of dense attention, and no latency, throughput, or peak-memory measurements are provided.

Evaluation is concentrated on CIFAR, synthetic Triangle/Sort-of-CLEVR, and a low-performing ImageNet100 subset. ImageNet100 and relational results lack repeated-run uncertainty; Oxford Pet is reported only as a curve; and comparisons omit stronger modern efficient vision or token-selection baselines. The visual specialization evidence also lacks a no-balance-loss control or quantitative per-slot analysis, so spatial patterns may simply reflect positional embeddings.

Reproducibility is further limited by contradictory learning rates (1e-5 in Section 4.1 versus 1e-4 in Table 8), no definition of the ImageNet100 class split/preprocessing, no grid-search space or validation protocol, and code being promised rather than provided. These are partly repairable reporting issues, but they compound the central procedural ambiguities.

Presentation-level refinements include tempering claims of a broadly 'sparse Transformer' and 'extensive' support: the core architecture still uses dense self-attention, and the current experiments do not substantiate general long-range association or large-scale efficiency. The batch-state ambiguity and incomplete mathematical definition, however, are material weaknesses rather than wording issues.

AiT consistently improves over the manuscript's matched ViT implementations: for example, AiT-Small obtains 83.34/56.30 on CIFAR-10/100 versus 79.53/53.19 for ViT-Small, while using 15.8M versus 14.9M parameters.

The component study is useful: removing memory, the bottleneck, the balance loss, Hopfield retrieval, or self-attention reduces average performance, and several results include means and standard deviations over three runs.
The paper provides parameter/FLOP counts, a beta sensitivity experiment, attention visualizations, and substantial appendix material, making the empirical behavior easier to examine.
weaknesses: Material: inference is batch-coupled and insufficiently defined. The method pools all B×N tokens, constructs memory from the whole batch, and uses an EWMA indexed by batch time. Consequently, a prediction may depend on other test samples, batch composition, order, and whether memory persists. The statement that memory is frozen during evaluation does not resolve how gamma^(t+1) is computed, while the test-time attention ablation indicates that the write pathway remains relevant. No B=1, batch-permutation, reset, or strictly inductive evaluation is reported, so the headline accuracies may not be comparable to ordinary per-example classification.

Material: key mathematics is not operationally well specified. Equation 5 combines quantities with incompatible matrix shapes and does not define the scalar reduction; Equation 6 states an exact argmin although implementation allegedly uses one update, whose formula is absent. The top-k scope and post-mask renormalization are also unspecified. Moreover, the load term based on 1(A>0) is either constant for dense softmax scores or nondifferentiable after hard masking, so it cannot provide the claimed training signal as written.

Material: the efficiency framing is not convincingly supported. AiT retains conventional quadratic self-attention and first computes dense memory-to-token scores before applying top-k. At matched depth it is slightly more expensive than ViT (e.g., 5.77G versus 5.60G FLOPs for Base), and no latency or memory measurements are given. Its apparent efficiency comes mainly from comparing a shallower AiT with a deeper, weakly trained ViT.

Material: experimental evidence is narrow and has weak absolute performance: the best CIFAR-10 result is 85.44%, ImageNet100 reaches only 36.72%, Oxford Pet is about 30%, and relational reasoning is evaluated only on the toy Sort-of-CLEVR benchmark. Comparisons focus on older or unusually weak reimplementations; there is no full ImageNet experiment or competitive contemporary vision/relational-reasoning baseline. This does not substantiate the broad performance, usefulness, or state-of-the-art claims.

Material: the Hopfield contribution is not isolated with a fair control. A one-step modern-Hopfield update is closely related to dot-product attention, but the reported replacement is a substantially more expensive multi-head cross-attention module that changes several factors simultaneously. Parameter/FLOP-matched tied-key/value attention and sensitivity to rank, memory size, top-k capacity, EWMA, and batch composition are missing.

strengths: The proposed Global Workspace Layer coherently combines low-rank priors, top-k memory writing, and continuous-Hopfield retrieval in a lightweight module. The motivation and overall architecture are understandable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2xh6td_7/call-fcf84f264b5f47be883550fb39f8872c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Within the authors' setup, matched-depth improvements are consistent: AiT-Small versus ViT-Small reaches 83.34% versus 79.53% on CIFAR-10 and 56.30% versus 53.19% on CIFAR-100; AiT-Medium reaches 36.72% versus 31.72% on ImageNet100.
The relational-reasoning results are promising: AiT-Base obtains 80.03% on relational Sort-of-CLEVR, compared with 73.43% for Coordination and 63.35% for ViT-Base.

The ablations examine most proposed components. The full small model averages 79.70%, versus 78.68% without the balance loss, 78.48% without Hopfield retrieval, and 73.75% without the bottleneck; initialization, energy, inverse-temperature, and attention visualizations provide additional diagnostic evidence.
weaknesses: Material concern: inference is nonstandard and batch-coupled. Section 3.2 concatenates all B×N tokens across examples, and settings such as k=512 exceed the token count of any single CIFAR image. Consequently, a prediction can use other test images. No B=1 result or sensitivity study over batch size, composition, and order is reported, so comparison with sample-independent baselines is not securely established.

The evaluation behavior of memory is internally unclear. Section 3.2 says explicit memory is frozen during evaluation, but Algorithm 1 updates it from each batch, while Appendix F shows that disabling cross-attention specifically at test time changes accuracy. The manuscript does not state whether test batches persistently update memory, form temporary batch-specific memory, or use only training-time memory; these alternatives imply materially different, potentially transductive protocols.

Several central equations are not technically executable as written. The load term uses an indicator (A>0): for the defined softmax A it is constant, while after top-k masking it has zero gradient almost everywhere, and no surrogate estimator is specified. The Hopfield energy mixes matrix and scalar quantities, omits an apparent transpose, and Equation 6 states an exact argmin although training reportedly uses one unspecified update. Top-k axes and the interaction between optimizer updates, EMA updates, and gradient detachment of the 'learnable' memory are also unspecified.

The efficiency claim is overstated. Every AiT block retains dense self-attention, and matched-depth AiT is larger and slightly more expensive than ViT: 15.8M/0.964G versus 14.9M/0.936G for Small and 45.9M/2.89G versus 42.7M/2.81G for Medium. Beating a deeper ViT demonstrates an empirical depth-accuracy tradeoff, but not improved asymptotic sparsity. No latency, peak-memory, or long-sequence experiment is given.

The Hopfield-specific contribution is not isolated fairly. A one-step modern Hopfield update is closely related to attention, while the replacement cross-attention baseline costs 1.19G FLOPs versus 0.964G for AiT. A parameter- and FLOP-matched attention retrieval baseline is needed before attributing the gain to associative-memory dynamics; the demonstrated energy decrease is expected from the chosen update.

Experimental support is limited relative to the broad claims. Absolute results are low on ImageNet100 (36.72%) and Oxford Pet (30.05%), full ImageNet and downstream vision tasks are absent, and stronger modern efficient-ViT or relational-reasoning baselines are not considered. Baselines are author reimplementations without reproduction checks, and key ImageNet100, Pet, and Sort-of-CLEVR results lack run-to-run uncertainty.

Reproducibility has concrete inconsistencies: Section 4.1 gives a learning rate of 1e-5 whereas Table 8 gives 1e-4; the ImageNet100 class subset is not defined; the validation protocol for the reported grid search, baseline-specific recipes, seeds, and precise test-time state handling are omitted; and code is only promised. These are consequential rather than cosmetic presentation issues.

strengths: The architecture is conceptually coherent: low-dimensional explicit memory, top-k writing, a balancing regularizer, and an associative read mechanism form a plausible approach to augmenting visual Transformers.

Matched-backbone results show consistent improvements over ViT on CIFAR-10/100. For example, AiT-Small improves from 79.53% to 83.34% on CIFAR-10 and from 53.19% to 56.30% on CIFAR-100, with three-run variability reported.

The component ablations are useful: removing memory recovers the ViT-Small result, while removing the balance loss, Hopfield read, or bottleneck reduces average accuracy by 1.02, 1.22, and 5.95 points, respectively. Parameter and FLOP counts are also reported.

The evaluation covers classification and synthetic relational reasoning, and the attention visualizations provide an initial qualitative indication that memory slots acquire different spatial preferences.
weaknesses: The central mathematical specification is not technically sound as written. In Eq. 5 and Algorithm 1, f_LT(gamma) has shape M x E while Xi has shape BN x E, so their stated product is undefined; Xi Xi^T is a BN x BN matrix rather than a scalar energy. Eq. 6 also gives only an argmin, not the actual one-step update used. These are consequential reproducibility and correctness issues for the principal mechanism.

The balance loss is ambiguous. A_i is defined as a softmax matrix, whose entries are strictly positive, making 1(A_i,j,o > 0) constant. The intended post-top-k mask, treatment of discarded weights, and renormalization are never formally defined, despite this loss and bottleneck being central to the reported gains.

The evaluation appears batch-composition dependent. Each memory update pools all B x N tokens, and Appendix Table 9 shows that disabling the write attention specifically at test time changes accuracy, contradicting the statement that memory is frozen during evaluation. Thus a prediction can depend on other test images in its batch and may also depend on evaluation order if the EWMA state persists. The reset protocol, single-sample behavior, and sensitivity to batch composition/order are not reported, so the standard independent-test interpretation of the results is not established.

The evidence for broad vision usefulness is limited. ImageNet-100 reaches only 36.72% and its exact subset and split are not defined; Oxford Pet reaches about 30%; Triangle is saturated and shows essentially no gain. ImageNet-100, Pet, and Sort-of-CLEVR results lack repeated-run uncertainty, and the comparison set omits stronger contemporary efficient vision Transformers and the canonical Relation Network for Sort-of-CLEVR.

The efficiency claims are overstated. AiT retains dense self-attention and adds a Global Workspace Layer; at matched depth it therefore has more parameters and FLOPs than ViT, such as 15.8M/0.964G versus 14.9M/0.936G for the Small models. Top-k is applied only after dense memory-to-token scores are computed. No long-sequence scaling, peak-memory, latency, or throughput evidence demonstrates a practical sparse-attention advantage.

The Hopfield ablation does not isolate associative-memory benefits. A one-step modern Hopfield read is closely related to softmax attention, while the replacement is a substantially heavier multi-head cross-attention model (1.19G versus 0.964G FLOPs). The observed difference therefore conflates parameterization and computation with the claimed energy-based retrieval property.

The specialization evidence is not controlled: Figures 6-8 show evolution during training but do not compare against the model without the balance loss or connect specialization quantitatively to relational accuracy. Consistent spatial masks could also arise from positional embeddings rather than abstract relational priors.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: code is only promised for future release, the main text specifies a learning rate of 1e-5 while Table 8 gives 1e-4, baseline training details are largely delegated to unspecified author-recommended settings, and the persistent-versus-ephemeral semantics of the memory update are unclear. These material concerns outweigh the interesting empirical gains, leading to a weak-reject recommendation.
